lesson.title: The Midnight Judge Who Gave the Supreme Court Its Power
lesson.summary: The 1803 case Marbury v. Madison, born out of the chaotic transition after the election of 1800, established judicial review and gave the Supreme Court the lasting power to strike down federal laws it finds unconstitutional.
lesson.body:
The roots of Marbury v. Madison trace back to the chaotic final weeks of John Adams's presidency, after Adams had lost the election of 1800 to Thomas Jefferson. Before leaving office in March 1801, the outgoing Federalist Congress passed the Judiciary Act of 1801, creating new federal judgeships, and Adams moved quickly to fill them with loyal Federalists, appointments that critics soon nicknamed the midnight judges because some commissions were reportedly signed and sealed right up until Adams's term ended.

One of these appointees was William Marbury, named a justice of the peace for the District of Columbia. His commission, however, was among a handful that had been signed and sealed but not yet physically delivered when Adams left office. When Jefferson became president, his new Secretary of State, James Madison, refused to deliver the outstanding commissions, since Jefferson had no interest in seating a wave of last minute Federalist appointees his predecessor had installed on the way out the door.

Marbury sued, asking the Supreme Court to issue a writ of mandamus, a court order compelling Madison to deliver his commission, relying on a provision of the Judiciary Act of 1789 that appeared to give the Supreme Court authority to issue such writs directly. Chief Justice John Marshall, himself a Federalist whom Adams had appointed in the final months of his presidency and who had briefly served as Adams's own Secretary of State, faced a genuinely delicate situation, ordering Madison to act might simply be ignored by the Jefferson administration, undermining the Court's authority, while refusing Marbury outright might look like caving to political pressure.

Marshall's ruling, issued in 1803, resolved the dilemma with a maneuver that reshaped American government. He agreed that Marbury had a right to his commission and that withholding it was wrong, but he then found that the provision of the Judiciary Act of 1789 giving the Supreme Court power to issue this kind of writ directly exceeded the original jurisdiction the Constitution itself granted the Court, and was therefore unconstitutional. As a result, Marshall ruled the Court had no authority to force delivery of the commission, and Marbury never got his job.

By striking down part of a federal law as unconstitutional, Marshall's opinion established the principle of judicial review, the power of federal courts to invalidate laws that conflict with the Constitution, a power the Constitution's text never explicitly granted but that has shaped nearly every major legal and political controversy in American history since. The case emerged directly from the bitter partisan transition of the election of 1800, and it ensured that even though Jefferson's party had won control of the presidency and Congress, the judiciary, still filled with Federalist appointees like Marshall, would remain a powerful and independent check on the other branches of government for generations to come.
